claim: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a progressive disease of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the retina leading to loss of central vision.
source: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a progressive disease of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the retina leading to loss of central vision.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about AMD that represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Polymorphisms in genes involved in lipid metabolism, including the ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), have been associated with AMD risk.
source: Polymorphisms in genes involved in lipid metabolism, including the ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), have been associated with AMD risk.
evidence: This statement references established genetic associations from prior research, as indicated by the citation context in the manuscript.

claim: Mutant mice lacking ABCA1 and ABCG1 in the RPE show lipid accumulation in the RPE.
source: Mutant mice show lipid accumulation in the RPE, reduced RPE and retinal function, retinal inflammation and RPE/photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in the generated mouse model, including histological staining and mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 2, 4, and 5.

claim: Mutant mice lacking ABCA1 and ABCG1 in the RPE show reduced RPE and retinal function.
source: Mutant mice show lipid accumulation in the RPE, reduced RPE and retinal function, retinal inflammation and RPE/photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings and rhodopsin regeneration kinetics data presented in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: Mutant mice lacking ABCA1 and ABCG1 in the RPE show retinal inflammation.
source: Mutant mice show lipid accumulation in the RPE, reduced RPE and retinal function, retinal inflammation and RPE/photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by IBA-1 staining and gene expression data for inflammatory markers shown in Figure 9.

claim: Mutant mice lacking ABCA1 and ABCG1 in the RPE show RPE/photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Mutant mice show lipid accumulation in the RPE, reduced RPE and retinal function, retinal inflammation and RPE/photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis, OCT imaging, and ONL thickness measurements shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: The ABCA1 AMD risk-conferring allele decreases ABCA1 expression in human cell lines.
source: Data from human cell lines indicate that the ABCA1 AMD risk-conferring allele decreases ABCA1 expression, identifying the potential molecular cause that underlies the genetic risk for AMD.
evidence: This is supported by mRNA and protein expression data from lymphoblastoid cell lines with different ABCA1 genotypes shown in Figure 11.

claim: Lipid efflux in the RPE plays an essential homeostatic role.
source: Our results highlight the essential homeostatic role for lipid efflux in the RPE and suggest a pathogenic contribution of reduced ABCA1 function to AMD.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the comprehensive phenotypic analysis of the knockout mouse model showing lipid accumulation, dysfunction, and degeneration.

claim: Reduced ABCA1 function may contribute pathogenically to AMD.
source: Our results highlight the essential homeostatic role for lipid efflux in the RPE and suggest a pathogenic contribution of reduced ABCA1 function to AMD.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the mouse model data and human genetic association, indicated by the word 'suggest'.

claim: AMD is the leading cause of blindness in the elderly population of Western countries.
source: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of blindness in the elderly population of Western countries (Klein et al., 2013; Joachim et al., 2015) and its socio-economic impact is predicted to dramatically increase in the next decades (Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: The socio-economic impact of AMD is predicted to dramatically increase in the next decades.
source: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of blindness in the elderly population of Western countries (Klein et al., 2013; Joachim et al., 2015) and its socio-economic impact is predicted to dramatically increase in the next decades (Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a predictive statement supported by a citation to Wong et al., 2014.

claim: AMD is a progressive disease of the macula, the central cone-rich region of the retina.
source: AMD is a progressive disease of the macula, the central cone-rich region of the retina, and can develop into the 'dry' or 'wet' form in the advanced stage.
evidence: This is a definitional statement representing established knowledge about AMD.

claim: AMD can develop into the 'dry' or 'wet' form in the advanced stage.
source: AMD is a progressive disease of the macula, the central cone-rich region of the retina, and can develop into the 'dry' or 'wet' form in the advanced stage.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about AMD classification.

claim: Dry AMD is characterized by atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Dry AMD is characterized by atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor degeneration, while wet AMD exhibits pathological neo-vascularization of the retina originating from the choroid.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about dry AMD pathology.

claim: Wet AMD exhibits pathological neo-vascularization of the retina originating from the choroid.
source: Dry AMD is characterized by atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor degeneration, while wet AMD exhibits pathological neo-vascularization of the retina originating from the choroid.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about wet AMD pathology.

claim: Both dry and wet AMD eventually result in loss of RPE and photoreceptors with deleterious consequences on high acuity and color vision.
source: Both conditions eventually result in loss of RPE and photoreceptors with deleterious consequences on high acuity and color vision (Bird et al., 1995; Lim et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The etiology of AMD is complex and multifactorial.
source: The etiology of AMD is complex and multifactorial but several lines of evidence associate the disease with local disturbances of lipid metabolism in the ageing human eye (Pauleikhoff et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a general statement about AMD etiology representing current scientific understanding.

claim: Several lines of evidence associate AMD with local disturbances of lipid metabolism in the ageing human eye.
source: The etiology of AMD is complex and multifactorial but several lines of evidence associate the disease with local disturbances of lipid metabolism in the ageing human eye (Pauleikhoff et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pauleikhoff et al., 1990.

claim: Lipids physiologically accumulate in extracellular deposits known as drusen and sub-retinal drusenoid deposits (SDDs) on the basal and apical side of the RPE, respectively.
source: Lipids physiologically accumulate in extracellular deposits known as drusen and sub-retinal drusenoid deposits (SDDs) on the basal and apical side of the RPE, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lipid deposits in the eye.

claim: Drusen contain polar lipids, such as un-esterified (free) cholesterol (UC) and phosphatidylcholine (PC), as well as neutral lipids, such as cholesteryl esters (CEs), and several lipid-binding proteins (apolipoproteins).
source: Drusen contain polar lipids, such as un-esterified (free) cholesterol (UC) and phosphatidylcholine (PC), as well as neutral lipids, such as cholesteryl esters (CEs), and several lipid-binding proteins (apolipoproteins) (Wang et al., 2010; Curcio et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement about drusen composition is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2010 and Curcio et al., 2011.

claim: SDDs seem to contain UC only, together with apolipoproteins.
source: The more recently identified SDDs, instead, seem to contain UC only, together with apolipoproteins (Rudolf et al., 2008; Spaide et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement about SDD composition is supported by citations and uses tentative language ('seem to').

claim: Drusen are considered hallmarks of AMD.
source: Drusen (Sarks, 1980) and SDDs (Zweifel et al., 2010) are considered hallmarks of AMD but their actual origin and contribution to the pathology remain unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sarks, 1980.

claim: SDDs are considered hallmarks of AMD.
source: Drusen (Sarks, 1980) and SDDs (Zweifel et al., 2010) are considered hallmarks of AMD but their actual origin and contribution to the pathology remain unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zweifel et al., 2010.

claim: The actual origin and contribution of drusen and SDDs to AMD pathology remain unknown.
source: Drusen (Sarks, 1980) and SDDs (Zweifel et al., 2010) are considered hallmarks of AMD but their actual origin and contribution to the pathology remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Primary RPE cells isolated from AMD patients, but not from control subjects, accumulate intracellular lipids in vitro.
source: Recently, primary RPE cells isolated from AMD patients, but not from control subjects, were shown to accumulate intracellular lipids in vitro (Golestaneh et al., 2017), suggesting altered lipid metabolism in diseased cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Golestaneh et al., 2017.

claim: Intracellular lipid accumulation in AMD patient-derived RPE cells suggests altered lipid metabolism in diseased cells.
source: Recently, primary RPE cells isolated from AMD patients, but not from control subjects, were shown to accumulate intracellular lipids in vitro (Golestaneh et al., 2017), suggesting altered lipid metabolism in diseased cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of lipid accumulation in AMD patient cells.

claim: Genome-wide association studies have linked AMD to several genes involved in generation and remodeling of high-density lipoproteins (HDLs), namely ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), apolipoprotein E (APOE), cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) and hepatic lipase C (LIPC).
source: Genome-wide association studies have linked AMD to several genes involved in generation and remodeling of high-density lipoproteins (HDLs), namely ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), apolipoprotein E (APOE), cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) and hepatic lipase C (LIPC) (Fritsche et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fritsche et al., 2016, a major GWAS study.

claim: Long-term elevated plasma levels of HDL-cholesterol are linked to increased AMD risk.
source: A recent review (van Leeuwen et al., 2018) summarizes contradictory results from different studies concerning the association between systemic lipid levels and the risk of developing AMD and links long-term elevated plasma levels of HDL-cholesterol to increased AMD risk.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to van Leeuwen et al., 2018.

claim: It remains unknown whether genes involved in lipid metabolism exert a local and/or a systemic pathogenic effect on the retina.
source: However, it remains unknown whether genes involved in lipid metabolism exert a local and/or a systemic pathogenic effect on the retina.
evidence: This is a statement about the current gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: ABCA1 encodes a transmembrane lipid transporter which generates HDLs together with its partner ABCG1.
source: A gene of interest in this context is ABCA1, encoding a transmembrane lipid transporter which generates HDLs together with its partner ABCG1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABCA1 and ABCG1 function.

claim: ABCA1 and ABCG1 use ATP to flip lipids, mainly UC and phospholipids (PLs), but also sphingomyelins (SMs) and oxysterols, from the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane to extracellular lipophilic acceptors.
source: Either transporter uses ATP to flip lipids, mainly UC and phospholipids (PLs), but also sphingomyelins (SMs) and oxysterols, from the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane to extracellular lipophilic acceptors such as apolipoproteins or nascent HDLs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of ABCA1 and ABCG1.

claim: ABCA1 initiates the formation of HDL by direct interaction with naked apolipoproteins.
source: ABCA1 initiates the formation of HDL by direct interaction with naked apolipoproteins, while ABCG1 requires a lipidated particle (Cavelier et al., 2006; Quazi and Molday, 2011; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cavelier et al., 2006; Quazi and Molday, 2011; Li et al., 2013.

claim: ABCG1 requires a lipidated particle for HDL formation.
source: ABCA1 initiates the formation of HDL by direct interaction with naked apolipoproteins, while ABCG1 requires a lipidated particle (Cavelier et al., 2006; Quazi and Molday, 2011; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cavelier et al., 2006; Quazi and Molday, 2011; Li et al., 2013.

claim: The ABCA1/ABCG1 pathway is also known as 'active cholesterol efflux'.
source: Since UC is one of the best established substrates of the two transporters, the ABCA1/ABCG1 pathway is also known as 'active cholesterol efflux'.
evidence: This is established terminology in the field.

claim: Mice lacking ABCA1, ABCG1 or both show macrophage foam cell formation.
source: The fundamental role of this pathway for cellular lipid homeostasis is highlighted by macrophage foam cell formation (Tabas, 2002; Favari et al., 2015) and by the progressive and age-dependent lung phenotype, including lipid accumulation in alveolar macrophages and pneumocytes, lung dysfunction and inflammation (Chai et al., 2017), in mice lacking ABCA1, ABCG1 or both.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tabas, 2002 and Favari et al., 2015.

claim: Mice lacking ABCA1, ABCG1 or both show progressive and age-dependent lung phenotype, including lipid accumulation in alveolar macrophages and pneumocytes, lung dysfunction and inflammation.
source: The fundamental role of this pathway for cellular lipid homeostasis is highlighted by macrophage foam cell formation (Tabas, 2002; Favari et al., 2015) and by the progressive and age-dependent lung phenotype, including lipid accumulation in alveolar macrophages and pneumocytes, lung dysfunction and inflammation (Chai et al., 2017), in mice lacking ABCA1, ABCG1 or both.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chai et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of cholesterol efflux leads to cell dysfunction in pancreatic beta cells.
source: Inhibition of cholesterol efflux leads to cell dysfunction also in pancreatic beta cells (Kruit et al., 2012), neurons (Karasinska et al., 2013) and liver cells (Arguello et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kruit et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of cholesterol efflux leads to cell dysfunction in neurons.
source: Inhibition of cholesterol efflux leads to cell dysfunction also in pancreatic beta cells (Kruit et al., 2012), neurons (Karasinska et al., 2013) and liver cells (Arguello et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Karasinska et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibition of cholesterol efflux leads to cell dysfunction in liver cells.
source: Inhibition of cholesterol efflux leads to cell dysfunction also in pancreatic beta cells (Kruit et al., 2012), neurons (Karasinska et al., 2013) and liver cells (Arguello et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Arguello et al., 2015.

claim: Liver X receptors (LXR) α and β are the upstream regulators of the ABCA1/ABCG1 pathway.
source: Liver X receptors (LXR) α and β are the upstream regulators of the pathway: these two transcription factors are activated upon binding of oxysterols that accumulate in conditions of increased UC and upregulate expression of both ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Schultz et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schultz et al., 2000.

claim: LXR transcription factors are activated upon binding of oxysterols that accumulate in conditions of increased UC.
source: Liver X receptors (LXR) α and β are the upstream regulators of the pathway: these two transcription factors are activated upon binding of oxysterols that accumulate in conditions of increased UC and upregulate expression of both ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Schultz et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schultz et al., 2000.

claim: LXR upregulate expression of both ABCA1 and ABCG1.
source: Liver X receptors (LXR) α and β are the upstream regulators of the pathway: these two transcription factors are activated upon binding of oxysterols that accumulate in conditions of increased UC and upregulate expression of both ABCA1 and ABCG1 (Schultz et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schultz et al., 2000.

claim: Ubiquitous expression of ABCA1 and ABCG1 has been reported in the mouse, monkey and human retina, including the RPE.
source: Ubiquitous expression of ABCA1 and ABCG1 has been reported in the mouse, monkey and human retina, including the RPE (Tserentsoodol et al., 2006; Duncan et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2012; Ananth et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2015; Storti et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to expression studies.

claim: ABCA1 and ABCG1 in the RPE mediate transport of UC to ApoA-I, ApoE, HDLs and human serum on both sides of the RPE.
source: The function of ABCA1 and ABCG1 in the RPE was previously investigated in vitro (Ishida et al., 2006; Duncan et al., 2009; Biswas et al., 2017; Storti et al., 2017; Lyssenko et al., 2018) and shown to mediate transport of UC to ApoA-I, ApoE, HDLs and human serum on both sides of the RPE.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple in vitro studies.

claim: ABCA1 and ABCG1 mediate transport of both plasma lipoprotein- and outer segment (OS)-derived cholesterol in the RPE.
source: This was true for plasma lipoprotein- as well as outer segment (OS)-derived cholesterol.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from the cited in vitro studies.

claim: The relevance of active cholesterol efflux for the RPE in vivo remains unknown.
source: However, the relevance of active cholesterol efflux for the RPE in vivo remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: The RPE needs an efficient metabolism to handle large amounts of lipids coming from daily OS phagocytosis.
source: This, together with the fact that the RPE needs an efficient metabolism to handle large amounts of lipids coming from daily OS phagocytosis (Strauss, 2005), prompted us to generate an RPE-specific Abca1;Abcg1 double knockout (KO) mouse.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Strauss, 2005.

claim: Expression of ABCA1 and ABCG1 throughout the retinal layers, including the RPE, was confirmed by immunofluorescence in wild type mouse retinal sections.
source: Expression of ABCA1 and ABCG1 throughout the retinal layers, including the RPE, was confirmed by immunofluorescence (IF) in wild type mouse retinal sections (Figure 1A) (Ananth et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and cited work by Ananth et al., 2014.

claim: ABCA1 and ABCG1 do not co-localize with ezrin (EZR), a marker of the apical microvilli of the RPE, in RPE cells.
source: As previously described for RPE cells in vitro (Storti et al., 2017), no co-localization with ezrin (EZR), a marker of the apical microvilli of the RPE, was observed.
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A and cited work by Storti et al., 2017.

claim: BEST1Cre mice express Cre recombinase under control of the human bestrophin 1 (BEST1) promoter, resulting in post-natal CRE activity specifically in the RPE.
source: BEST1Cre mice express Cre recombinase under control of the human bestrophin 1 (BEST1, also known as vitelliform macular dystrophy 2, VMD2) promoter, resulting in post-natal CRE activity specifically in the RPE (Iacovelli et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Iacovelli et al., 2011.

claim: High mRNA levels for Cre were detected in the eyecup (RPE/choroid) with only a minimal amount of transcripts found in the neural retina in RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
source: High mRNA levels for Cre were detected in the eyecup (RPE/choroid) with only a minimal amount of transcripts found in the neural retina, probably due to contamination during eye dissection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CRE-positive nuclei were detected only in the RPE layer of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 but not of control (Ctr, Cre-negative) mice.
source: Although some un-specific staining was observed in the inner retina, CRE-positive nuclei were detected only in the RPE layer of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 but not of control (Ctr, Cre-negative) mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Deletion of Abca1 and Abcg1 was observed in eyecups, but not neural retinas, of Cre-positive mice.
source: As expected, deletion of Abca1 and Abcg1 was observed in eyecups, but not neural retinas, of Cre-positive mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The BEST1Cre mouse is known to have patchy and variable Cre expression in the RPE.
source: Of note, the BEST1Cre mouse is known to have patchy and variable Cre expression in the RPE (Iacovelli et al., 2011; Sundermeier et al., 2017), which could partially explain decreased rather than abolished expression of Abca1 and Abcg1 mRNA in eyecups of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Iacovelli et al., 2011 and Sundermeier et al., 2017.

claim: At 2 months of age, the fundus of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 but not of Ctr mice showed a dotted pattern, possibly reflecting alterations in the pigmentation of RPE cells.
source: Already at 2 months of age, the fundus of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 but not of Ctr mice showed a dotted pattern, possibly reflecting alterations in the pigmentation of RPE cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by fundus imaging data shown in Figure 2A, with speculative interpretation.

claim: Light and electron microscopy on retinal sections revealed an irregular apical RPE border and accumulation of intracellular material resembling lipid droplets in RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 but not Ctr mice.
source: Light and electron microscopy on retinal sections revealed an irregular apical RPE border and accumulation of intracellular material resembling lipid droplets (LDs) in RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 but not Ctr mice (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Staining with OilRedO in retinal sections revealed strong lipid accumulation in CRE-positive RPE cells of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
source: Staining with OilRedO (ORO) in retinal sections (Figure 2D) and LipidTOX in RPE flat mounts (Figure 2E) revealed strong lipid accumulation in CRE-positive RPE cells of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by ORO staining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Staining with LipidTOX in RPE flat mounts revealed strong lipid accumulation in CRE-positive RPE cells of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
source: Staining with OilRedO (ORO) in retinal sections (Figure 2D) and LipidTOX in RPE flat mounts (Figure 2E) revealed strong lipid accumulation in CRE-positive RPE cells of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by LipidTOX staining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CRE-negative RPE cells and other retinal layers were ORO-negative and served as internal controls demonstrating the specificity of lipid accumulation in RPE cells lacking Abca1 and/or Abcg1.
source: CRE-negative RPE cells and other retinal layers were ORO-negative and served as internal controls demonstrating the specificity of lipid accumulation in RPE cells lacking Abca1 and/or Abcg1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ORO staining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both ORO and LipidTOX stain neutral lipids, which constitute the hydrophobic core of LDs.
source: Both ORO and LipidTOX stain neutral lipids, which constitute the hydrophobic core of LDs (Olofsson et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Olofsson et al., 2009.

claim: Actin staining of RPE flat mounts showed morphological irregularities of CRE-positive cells in RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice when compared to the regular, mainly hexagonal shape of Ctr cells.
source: Moreover, actin staining of RPE flat mounts showed morphological irregularities of CRE-positive cells in RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice when compared to the regular, mainly hexagonal shape of Ctr cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by actin staining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Morphological irregularities in RPE cells progressively worsened and were more pronounced at 4–6 months of age.
source: These morphological irregularities progressively worsened and were more pronounced at 4–6 months of age (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Double staining for ZO-1 and β-catenin in mutant cells revealed re-localization of β-cat from the plasma membrane to the cytosol, a feature of disorganized RPE.
source: In particular, double staining for the tight junction protein zona occludens 1 (ZO-1) and the Wnt signaling mediator β-catenin (β-cat) in mutant cells revealed re-localization of β-cat from the plasma membrane to the cytosol, a feature of disorganized RPE (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and cited work by Yang et al., 2018.

claim: Pigment epithelial cells in 4 months old RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice were significantly larger and irregularly shaped.
source: Pigment epithelial cells in 4 months old RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice were significantly larger and irregularly shaped (Figure 3A, quantification in 3B and 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative morphometric analysis shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: At 6 months, areas of dysmorphic RPE with accumulation of intracellular material and areas of RPE atrophy with infiltration of inflammatory cells were observed in mutant but not control mice.
source: At 6 months, we observed areas of dysmorphic RPE with accumulation of intracellular material and areas of RPE atrophy with infiltration of inflammatory cells (see below) in mutant but not control mice (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Photoreceptor loss correlated with RPE atrophy.
source: Photoreceptor loss correlated with RPE atrophy (see below).
evidence: This is an inference from the morphological observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Variability of the phenotype within the same retina was probably due to patchy Cre expression.
source: Variability of the phenotype within the same retina was probably due to patchy Cre expression (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed phenotypic variability.

claim: Reduced expression levels of Cre and the RPE marker monocarboxylic acid transporter 3 (Mct3) indicated atrophic RPE at 6 months of age.
source: Reduced expression levels of Cre and the RPE marker monocarboxylic acid transporter 3 (Mct3) further indicated atrophic RPE at 6 months of age (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Loss of RPE cells in aged RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice was most likely a consequence of the lack of ABCA1 and/or ABCG1 activity in RPE rather than of CRE expression per se.
source: Loss of RPE cells in aged RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice was most likely a consequence of the lack of ABCA1 and/or ABCG1 activity in RPE rather than of CRE expression per se, since Cre mRNA levels declined in eyecups of old RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 (Figure 3F) but not old BEST1Cre mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of Cre expression levels in different mouse strains shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Morphological abnormalities of RPE cells in RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice were not due to potential CRE toxicity.
source: Similarly, morphological abnormalities of RPE cells in RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice were not due to potential CRE toxicity (Thanos et al., 2012; He et al., 2014) as BEST1Cre mice only showed minor morphological alterations in the RPE and few bright spots in the fundus, but no lipid accumulation or functional changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of BEST1Cre control mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citations to Thanos et al., 2012 and He et al., 2014.

claim: Lack of Abca1 and/or Abcg1 resulted in lipid accumulation in the RPE and led to several morphological abnormalities that aggravated with time and eventually resulted in RPE cell death.
source: Thus, lack of Abca1 and/or Abcg1 resulted in lipid accumulation in the RPE and led to several morphological abnormalities that aggravated with time and eventually resulted in RPE cell death.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the morphological and functional data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Lipid accumulation was observed in adult RPE cells lacking Abca1 and/or Abcg1 after AAV-mediated gene deletion.
source: Although expression levels of GFP were variable and difficult to detect in some individual cells, LDs were specifically observed in GFP-positive (transduced) cells by LipidTOX staining 10 weeks after AAV injection (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by AAV transduction experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: RPE cells in the AAV-transduced area appeared larger and less regular than in the non-transduced area, similar to the morphological alterations detected in RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
source: In addition, RPE cells in the transduced area appeared larger and less regular than in the non-transduced area, similar to the morphological alterations detected in RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis of AAV-transduced RPE shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Lipid accumulation in GFP-positive RPE of Abca1flox/flox;Abcg1flox/flox mice was confirmed in retinal sections, which showed ORO-positive lipid staining specifically in the RPE of transduced areas.
source: Lipid accumulation in GFP-positive RPE of Abca1flox/flox;Abcg1flox/flox mice was further confirmed in retinal sections, which showed ORO-positive lipid staining specifically in the RPE of transduced areas, as well as co-localization of GFP and CRE signals (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is supported by ORO staining and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 4C-F.

claim: Altered morphology and intracellular lipid accumulation occur in adult RPE cells lacking Abca1 and/or Abcg1.
source: Taken together, these data indicated altered morphology and intracellular lipid accumulation in adult RPE cells lacking Abca1 and/or Abcg1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the AAV transduction experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The phenotype of lipid accumulation in adult RPE cells is in agreement with the known function of ABCA1/ABCG1 as mediators of lipid efflux in the RPE.
source: This phenotype is in agreement with the known function of ABCA1/ABCG1 as mediators of lipid efflux in the RPE.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed phenotype to known protein function.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed significantly increased concentration of CEs in eyecups of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
source: The analysis revealed significantly increased concentration of CEs in eyecups of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: UC, PLs, sphingolipids (SLs) including sphingomyelins (SMs) and ceramides (Cer), and glycerolipids (GLs) including diacylglycerols (DAGs) and triglycerides (TGs) remained unchanged in eyecups of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
source: In contrast UC, PLs, sphingolipids (SLs) including sphingomyelins (SMs) and ceramides (Cer), and glycerolipids (GLs) including diacylglycerols (DAGs) and triglycerides (TGs) remained unchanged (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: All of the individual CE species analyzed were more abundant in the mutant mice compared to control littermates.
source: All of the individual CE species analyzed were more abundant in the mutant mice compared to control littermates.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Some CE species were dramatically increased up to 100 fold in eyecups of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
source: Some CE species were dramatically increased up to 100 fold (Figure 5B), including CEs containing fatty acid chains typically found in the retina such as palmitic (16:0), oleic (18:1) and docosahexaenoic (22:6) acid, which is the most abundant fatty acid of photoreceptor OS (Fliesler and Anderson, 1983; Martin et al., 2005; Bretillon et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CEs containing fatty acid chains typically found in the retina such as palmitic (16:0), oleic (18:1) and docosahexaenoic (22:6) acid were increased in eyecups of RPEΔAbca1;Abcg1 mice.
